Model 1:
# Train Rescheduling and Speed Management Problem (TRSMP) — Complete MILP Formulation

Below is the full mixed-integer linear program. All nonlinear terms (notably $v^2$ in the energy function) have been linearized via standard techniques (piecewise-linear approximation with binary selection variables and big-M).

---

## 1. Sets

| Symbol | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| $T$ | Set of trains, indexed by $t, t'$ |
| $S$ | Set of stations, indexed by $s$ |
| $K$ | Set of track segments, indexed by $k$ |
| $B_k$ | Set of blocks within segment $k$, indexed by $b$ |
| $I$ | Set of discrete time intervals, indexed by $i$ |
| $D=\{1,2\}$ | Set of travel directions (1 = nominal, 2 = opposite) |
| $N$ | Set of piecewise-linear segments for the $v^2$ approximation, indexed by $n$ |

---

## 2. Parameters

| Symbol | Description | Unit |
|--------|-------------|------|
| $L_k$ | Length of segment $k$ | km |
| $L_{k,b}$ | Length of block $b$ in segment $k$ | km |
| $v_{\max}, v_{\min}$ | Maximum / minimum allowable speed | km/h |
| $a_{\max}, b_{\max}$ | Maximum acceleration / deceleration | km/h per interval |
| $\tau$ | Minimum headway time | min |
| $t_d^{\text{start}}, t_d^{\text{end}}$ | Start / end of disruption window | interval index |
| $k_d$ | Disrupted segment | — |
| $\text{dir}_d \in D$ | Direction affected by disruption | — |
| $\text{dwell}_{\min}, \text{dwell}_{\max}$ | Min / max dwell time at stations | min |
| $e_0, e_1, e_2, e_3$ | Energy consumption coefficients | — |
| $\text{sch\_arr}_{t,s}, \text{sch\_dep}_{t,s}$ | Scheduled arrival / departure time | min |
| $o_t, \text{dst}_t$ | Origin / destination station of train $t$ | — |
| $\text{dir}_t \in D$ | Nominal direction of train $t$ | — |
| $M$ | Sufficiently large positive constant (big-M) | — |
| $\Delta t$ | Duration of one time interval | min |
| $v_n^L, v_n^U$ | Lower / upper speed bound of PWL segment $n$ | km/h |
| $\alpha_n, \beta_n$ | Slope / intercept of $v^2$ approximation on segment $n$ | — |
| $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ | Objective weights for delay, energy, cancellation | — |

---

## 3. Decision Variables

| Variable | Domain | Description |
|----------|--------|-------------|
| $x_{t,k,b,i}$ | $\{0,1\}$ | 1 if train $t$ occupies block $b$ of segment $k$ in interval $i$ |
| $v_{t,k,b,i}$ | $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ | Speed of train $t$ in block $(k,b)$ during interval $i$ |
| $a_{t,k,b,i}$ | $\mathbb{R}$ | Acceleration of train $t$ in block $(k,b)$ during interval $i$ |
| $\text{arr}_{t,s}$ | $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ | Actual arrival time of train $t$ at station $s$ |
| $\text{dep}_{t,s}$ | $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ | Actual departure time of train $t$ at station $s$ |
| $\text{delay}_{t,s}$ | $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ | Delay of train $t$ at station $s$ |
| $e_{t,k,b,i}$ | $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ | Energy consumed by train $t$ in block $(k,b)$ during interval $i$ |
| $w_{t,k,b,i}$ | $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ | Auxiliary variable $\approx v_{t,k,b,i}^2$ |
| $z_{t,k,b,i,n}$ | $\{0,1\}$ | 1 if PWL segment $n$ is active for the $v^2$ approximation |
| $y_{t,t',k,b,i}$ | $\{0,1\}$ | 1 if train $t$ precedes train $t'$ in block $(k,b)$ at interval $i$ |
| $r_{t,k}$ | $\{0,1\}$ | 1 if train $t$ is rerouted (uses opposite track) on segment $k$ |
| $\text{cancel}_t$ | $\{0,1\}$ | 1 if train $t$ is cancelled |

---

## 4. Objective Function

$$
\min \; Z \;=\; \alpha \sum_{t \in T}\sum_{s \in S} \text{delay}_{t,s} \;+\; \beta \sum_{t \in T}\sum_{k \in K}\sum_{b \in B_k}\sum_{i \in I} e_{t,k,b,i} \;+\; \gamma \sum_{t \in T} \text{cancel}_t
$$

---

## 5. Constraints

### 5.1 Block Occupation (one train per block-time-direction)

$$
\sum_{\substack{t \in T \\ \text{dir}_t = d}} x_{t,k,b,i} \;\le\; 1 \qquad \forall\, k \in K,\; b \in B_k,\; i \in I,\; d \in D
$$

### 5.2 Bidirectional Conflict (opposite-direction trains cannot share a block)

$$
x_{t,k,b,i} + x_{t',k,b,i} \;\le\; 1 \qquad \forall\, t,t' \in T:\; \text{dir}_t \neq \text{dir}_{t'},\; k \in K,\; b \in B_k,\; i \in I
$$

### 5.3 Flow Conservation (sequential block traversal within a segment)

$$
x_{t,k,b,i} \;\le\; x_{t,k,b-1,i} \qquad \forall\, t \in T,\; k \in K,\; b \in B_k \setminus \{1\},\; i \in I
$$

### 5.4 Train Dynamics (speed update)

$$
v_{t,k,b,i+1} \;=\; v_{t,k,b,i} + a_{t,k,b,i}\,\Delta t \qquad \forall\, t \in T,\; k \in K,\; b \in B_k,\; i \in I \setminus \{|I|\}
$$

### 5.5 Speed Limits

$$
v_{\min}\,x_{t,k,b,i} \;\le\; v_{t,k,b,i} \;\le\; v_{\max}\,x_{t,k,b,i} \qquad \forall\, t \in T,\; k \in K,\; b \in B_k,\; i \in I
$$

### 5.6 Acceleration Limits

$$
-b_{\max} \;\le\; a_{t,k,b,i} \;\le\; a_{\max} \qquad \forall\, t \in T,\; k \in K,\; b \in B_k,\; i \in I
$$

### 5.7 Dwell Time at Stations

$$
\text{dwell}_{\min} \;\le\; \text{dep}_{t,s} - \text{arr}_{t,s} \;\le\; \text{dwell}_{\max} \qquad \forall\, t \in T,\; s \in S
$$

### 5.8 Disruption (blocked segment/direction during disruption window)

$$
x_{t,k_d,b,i} \;=\; 0 \qquad \forall\, t \in T:\; \text{dir}_t = \text{dir}_d,\; b \in B_{k_d},\; i \in I:\; t_d^{\text{start}} \le i \le t_d^{\text{end}}
$$

### 5.9 Rerouting (if $r_{t,k}=1$, train uses opposite physical track)

Define the physical track used by train $t$ on segment $k$ as $p_{t,k} \in \{0,1\}$ (0 = track for direction 2, 1 = track for direction 1), where $p_{t,k} = \text{dir}_t \oplus r_{t,k}$ (XOR). Linearization:

$$
\begin{aligned}
p_{t,k} &\ge \text{dir}_t - r_{t,k} \\
p_{t,k} &\ge r_{t,k} - \text{dir}_t \\
p_{t,k} &\le \text{dir}_t + r_{t,k} \\
p_{t,k} &\le 2 - \text{dir}_t - r_{t,k}
\end{aligned}
\qquad \forall\, t \in T,\; k \in K
$$

Bidirectional conflict on the same physical track (replaces 5.2):

$$
x_{t,k,b,i} + x_{t',k,b,i} \;\le\; 1 + M\,|p_{t,k} - p_{t',k}| \qquad \forall\, t,t' \in T,\; k \in K,\; b \in B_k,\; i \in I
$$

with $|p_{t,k} - p_{t',k}|$ linearized via auxiliary variable $\delta_{t,t',k} \in \{0,1\}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\delta_{t,t',k} &\ge p_{t,k} - p_{t',k} \\
\delta_{t,t',k} &\ge p_{t',k} - p_{t,k} \\
|p_{t,k} - p_{t',k}| &= \delta_{t,t',k}
\end{aligned}
$$

### 5.10 Delay Definition

$$
\text{delay}_{t,s} \;\ge\; \text{arr}_{t,s} - \text{sch\_arr}_{t,s} \qquad \forall\, t \in T,\; s \in S
$$

### 5.11 Origin / Destination Pinning

$$
\text{arr}_{t,o_t} = \text{sch\_arr}_{t,o_t}, \qquad \text{dep}_{t,\text{dst}_t} = \text{sch\_dep}_{t,\text{dst}_t} \qquad \forall\, t \in T
$$

### 5.12 Energy Consumption (linearized)

$$
e_{t,k,b,i} \;=\; \bigl(e_0 + e_1\,v_{t,k,b,i} + e_2\,w_{t,k,b,i} + e_3\,a_{t,k,b,i}\bigr)\,\Delta t \qquad \forall\, t \in T,\; k \in K,\; b \in B_k,\; i \in I
$$

**Piecewise-linear approximation of $w = v^2$:**

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\sum_{n \in N} z_{t,k,b,i,n} = 1 &&\forall\, t,k,b,i \\
&v_n^L\,z_{t,k,b,i,n} \le v_{t,k,b,i} \le v_n^U\,z_{t,k,b,i,n} &&\forall\, t,k,b,i,\; n \in N \\
&w_{t,k,b,i} \ge \alpha_n\,v_{t,k,b,i} + \beta_n - M\,(1 - z_{t,k,b,i,n}) &&\forall\, t,k,b,i,\; n \in N \\
&w_{t,k,b,i} \le \alpha_n\,v_{t,k,b,i} + \beta_n + M\,(1 - z_{t,k,b,i,n}) &&\forall\, t,k,b,i,\; n \in N
\end{aligned}
$$

### 5.13 Headway at Stations (same direction)

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{arr}_{t',s} - \text{arr}_{t,s} &\ge \tau - M\,(1 - y_{t,t',s}) \\
\text{arr}_{t,s} - \text{arr}_{t',s} &\ge \tau - M\,y_{t,t',s} \\
y_{t,t',s} + y_{t',t,s} &= 1
\end{aligned}
\qquad \forall\, t,t' \in T:\; \text{dir}_t = \text{dir}_{t'},\; s \in S
$$

### 5.14 Block-Level Ordering (conflicting trains)

$$
y_{t,t',k,b,i} + y_{t',t,k,b,i} = 1 \qquad \forall\, t,t' \in T:\; t \neq t',\; k \in K,\; b \in B_k,\; i \in I
$$

with the linking constraint:

$$
x_{t,k,b,i} + x_{t',k,b,i} - 1 \;\le\; y_{t,t',k,b,i} + y_{t',t,k,b,i} \qquad \forall\, t,t' \in T,\; k \in K,\; b \in B_k,\; i \in I
$$

### 5.15 Cancellation

$$
x_{t,k,b,i} \;\le\; 1 - \text{cancel}_t \qquad \forall\, t \in T,\; k \in K,\; b \in B_k,\; i \in I
$$

### 5.16 Arrival/Departure Consistency

$$
\text{arr}_{t,s} \;\le\; \text{dep}_{t,s} \qquad \forall\, t \in T,\; s \in S
$$

$$
\text{arr}_{t,s+1} \;\ge\; \text{dep}_{t,s} \qquad \forall\, t \in T,\; s \in S \setminus \{|S|\}
$$

### 5.17 Block Traversal Time (speed–distance consistency)

$$
v_{t,k,b,i}\,\Delta t \;\le\; L_{k,b} + M\,(1 - x_{t,k,b,i}) \qquad \forall\, t \in T,\; k \in K,\; b \in B_k,\; i \in I
$$

### 5.18 Minimum Block Coverage (each block must be occupied long enough)

$$
\sum_{i \in I} x_{t,k,b,i} \;\ge\; \left\lceil \frac{L_{k,b}}{v_{\max}\,\Delta t} \right\rceil (1 - \text{cancel}_t) \qquad \forall\, t \in T,\; k \in K,\; b \in B_k
$$

### 5.19 Segment Entry/Exit (train must traverse every segment if not cancelled)

$$
\sum_{b \in B_k}\sum_{i \in I} x_{t,k,1,i} \;\ge\; 1 - \text{cancel}_t, \qquad \sum_{b \in B_k}\sum_{i \in I} x_{t,k,|B_k|,i} \;\ge\; 1 - \text{cancel}_t \qquad \forall\, t \in T,\; k \in K
$$

---

## 6. Explanation of Key Modeling Choices

| Element | Modeling rationale |
|---------|--------------------|
| **Time discretization** | The horizon is discretized into intervals of length $\Delta t$. This converts the continuous-time motion into a combinatorial problem suitable for MILP. |
| **Block occupation $x_{t,k,b,i}$** | Binary variable that captures both *where* and *when* a train is. All safety constraints (occupancy, headway, bidirectional conflict) are expressed through it. |
| **Speed/acceleration variables** | Indexed by $(t,k,b,i)$ so that the dynamics equation (5.4) is a pure linear recurrence. The big-M in (5.5) forces $v=0$ when the block is unoccupied. |
| **Energy linearization (5.12)** | The quadratic term $v^2$ is replaced by $w$ and approximated by a piecewise-linear function over $N$ segments. The binary $z_{t,k,b,i,n}$ selects the active segment; the four constraints enforce that $w$ equals the linear approximation on the active segment and is unconstrained otherwise. |
| **Rerouting (5.9)** | The XOR between $\text{dir}_t$ and $r_{t,k}$ is linearized with four inequalities defining $p_{t,k}$. The bidirectional conflict then uses $|p_{t,k}-p_{t',k}|$ (linearized via $\delta$) so that only trains on the *same physical track* compete for a block. |
| **Ordering variables $y$** | Used both at the station level (5.13) for headway and at the block level (5.14) to break symmetry between trains that would otherwise compete for the same resource. |
| **Cancellation (5.15)** | A single binary $\text{cancel}_t$ zeroes out all block occupations and contributes $\gamma$ to the objective, allowing the optimizer to trade off cancellation vs. delay/energy. |
| **Disruption (5.8)** | Directly forces $x=0$ for the affected segment, direction, and time window — the partial blockage is therefore "hard" (infeasible to traverse). |
| **Big-M usage** | All big-M terms are tightened by the natural bounds of the variables (e.g., $M \ge |I|\,\Delta t$ for time differences, $M \ge v_{\max}^2$ for the PWL approximation) to keep the LP relaxation strong. |

This model is a complete, linear MILP ready to be passed to any standard MILP solver (Gurobi, CPLEX, SCIP, HiGHS, etc.). The size of the instance is governed by $|T|\cdot|K|\cdot|B_k|\cdot|I|$ binary variables (block occupations) plus $|T|\cdot|K|\cdot|B_k|\cdot|I|\cdot|N|$ additional binaries for the PWL energy approximation.

Model 2:
# Train Rescheduling and Speed Management Problem (TRSMP) — Complete MILP Formulation

Below is the full mixed-integer linear program. All nonlinear terms (notably $v^2$) are linearized via a piecewise-linear (PWL) approximation with breakpoints, and all logical/implication conditions are encoded with big-M.

---

## 1. Sets

| Symbol | Description |
|---|---|
| $T$ | Set of trains, indexed by $t$ |
| $S$ | Set of stations, indexed by $s$ |
| $K$ | Set of segments, indexed by $k$ |
| $B_k$ | Set of blocks in segment $k$, indexed by $b$ |
| $I$ | Set of discrete time intervals, indexed by $i$ |
| $D=\{1,2\}$ | Directions (1 = nominal, 2 = opposite) |
| $P$ | Set of breakpoints for PWL of $v^2$, indexed by $p$ |

Auxiliary index sets:
- $I^{d} = \{i \in I : t_d^{\text{start}} \le i \le t_d^{\text{end}}\}$ — disruption window
- $T^{d} = \{t \in T : \text{dir}_t = \text{dir}_d\}$ — trains affected by disruption
- $\text{prev}(k,b), \text{next}(k,b)$ — predecessor/successor block of $(k,b)$ along the track

---

## 2. Parameters

| Symbol | Description |
|---|---|
| $L_k$ | Length of segment $k$ |
| $L_{k,b}$ | Length of block $b$ in segment $k$ |
| $v^{\max}, v^{\min}$ | Maximum / minimum speed |
| $a^{\max}, b^{\max}$ | Maximum acceleration / deceleration |
| $\tau$ | Minimum headway time |
| $t_d^{\text{start}}, t_d^{\text{end}}$ | Start/end of disruption window |
| $k_d$ | Disrupted segment |
| $\text{dir}_d$ | Disrupted direction |
| $\text{dwell}^{\min}, \text{dwell}^{\max}$ | Min/max dwell time at stations |
| $e_0, e_1, e_2, e_3$ | Energy consumption coefficients |
| $\text{sch\_arr}_{t,s}, \text{sch\_dep}_{t,s}$ | Scheduled arrival/departure times |
| $o_t, \text{dst}_t$ | Origin / destination station of train $t$ |
| $\text{dir}_t$ | Nominal direction of train $t$ |
| $M$ | Large positive constant (big-M) |
| $\Delta t$ | Duration of one time interval |
| $v_p, v_p^{\text{sq}}$ | Speed at breakpoint $p$ and its square ($v_p^{\text{sq}} = v_p^2$) |

---

## 3. Decision Variables

| Variable | Domain | Description |
|---|---|---|
| $x_{t,k,b,i}$ | $\{0,1\}$ | 1 if train $t$ occupies block $(k,b)$ at interval $i$ |
| $v_{t,k,b,i}$ | $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ | Speed of train $t$ in block $(k,b)$ at interval $i$ |
| $a_{t,k,b,i}$ | $\mathbb{R}$ | Acceleration of train $t$ in block $(k,b)$ at interval $i$ |
| $\text{arr}_{t,s}$ | $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ | Actual arrival time of train $t$ at station $s$ |
| $\text{dep}_{t,s}$ | $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ | Actual departure time of train $t$ at station $s$ |
| $\text{delay}_{t,s}$ | $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ | Delay of train $t$ at station $s$ |
| $e_{t,k,b,i}$ | $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ | Energy consumed by train $t$ in block $(k,b)$ at $i$ |
| $y_{t,t',k,b,i}$ | $\{0,1\}$ | 1 if $t$ is ordered before $t'$ in block $(k,b)$ at $i$ |
| $r_{t,k}$ | $\{0,1\}$ | 1 if train $t$ is rerouted in segment $k$ |
| $\text{cancel}_t$ | $\{0,1\}$ | 1 if train $t$ is cancelled |
| $\lambda_{t,k,b,i,p}$ | $[0,1]$ | PWL weight for breakpoint $p$ |
| $v^{\text{sq}}_{t,k,b,i}$ | $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ | Auxiliary variable equal to $v_{t,k,b,i}^2$ |

---

## 4. Objective Function

$$
\min \; \alpha \sum_{t \in T}\sum_{s \in S} \text{delay}_{t,s} \;+\; \beta \sum_{t \in T}\sum_{k \in K}\sum_{b \in B_k}\sum_{i \in I} e_{t,k,b,i} \;+\; \gamma \sum_{t \in T} \text{cancel}_t
$$

where $\alpha, \beta, \gamma \ge 0$ are weighting coefficients.

---

## 5. Constraints

### 5.1 Block Occupation (single train per block-time per direction)

$$
\sum_{t \in T : \text{dir}_t = d} x_{t,k,b,i} \;\le\; 1 \qquad \forall\, k \in K,\; b \in B_k,\; i \in I,\; d \in D
$$

### 5.2 Bidirectional Conflict (opposite directions cannot share a block)

$$
x_{t,k,b,i} + x_{t',k,b,i} \;\le\; 1 \qquad \forall\, t,t' \in T,\; \text{dir}_t \ne \text{dir}_{t'},\; k \in K,\; b \in B_k,\; i \in I
$$

### 5.3 Flow Conservation (sequential movement through blocks)

A train may occupy block $(k,b)$ at time $i$ only if it was in $(k,b)$ or in a predecessor block at $i-1$:

$$
x_{t,k,b,i} \;\le\; x_{t,k,b,i-1} + x_{t,\text{prev}(k,b),i-1} \qquad \forall\, t \in T,\; k \in K,\; b \in B_k,\; i \in I \setminus \{0\}
$$

A train in $(k,b)$ at $i-1$ must be in $(k,b)$ or a successor block at $i$:

$$
x_{t,k,b,i-1} \;\le\; x_{t,k,b,i} + x_{t,\text{next}(k,b),i} \qquad \forall\, t \in T,\; k \in K,\; b \in B_k,\; i \in I \setminus \{0\}
$$

(For boundary blocks, $\text{prev}$ or $\text{next}$ is null and the corresponding term is dropped.)

### 5.4 Train Dynamics (speed update)

$$
v_{t,k,b,i+1} \;=\; v_{t,k,b,i} + a_{t,k,b,i}\,\Delta t \qquad \forall\, t \in T,\; k \in K,\; b \in B_k,\; i \in I \setminus \{\max I\}
$$

### 5.5 Speed Limits

$$
v^{\min}\, x_{t,k,b,i} \;\le\; v_{t,k,b,i} \;\le\; v^{\max}\, x_{t,k,b,i} \qquad \forall\, t,k,b,i
$$

### 5.6 Acceleration Limits

$$
-b^{\max}\, x_{t,k,b,i} \;\le\; a_{t,k,b,i} \;\le\; a^{\max}\, x_{t,k,b,i} \qquad \forall\, t,k,b,i
$$

### 5.7 Dwell Time at Stations

$$
\text{dwell}^{\min} \;\le\; \text{dep}_{t,s} - \text{arr}_{t,s} \;\le\; \text{dwell}^{\max} \qquad \forall\, t \in T,\; s \in S
$$

### 5.8 Disruption (blocked segment/direction/window)

Trains whose nominal direction equals the disrupted direction cannot occupy the disrupted segment during the disruption window unless they are rerouted:

$$
x_{t,k_d,b,i} \;\le\; r_{t,k_d} \qquad \forall\, t \in T^{d},\; b \in B_{k_d},\; i \in I^{d}
$$

### 5.9 Rerouting (use opposite track)

If $r_{t,k}=1$, train $t$ uses the opposite-direction track in segment $k$. The bidirectional conflict (5.2) is therefore conditioned on the *effective* direction:

$$
\text{eff\_dir}_{t,k} \;=\; \text{dir}_t\,(1 - r_{t,k}) + (3 - \text{dir}_t)\,r_{t,k}
$$

The conflict constraint becomes:

$$
x_{t,k,b,i} + x_{t',k,b,i} \;\le\; 1 + M\bigl(1 - [\text{eff\_dir}_{t,k} = \text{eff\_dir}_{t',k}]\bigr) \qquad \forall\, t,t',k,b,i
$$

where $[\cdot]$ is the indicator (linearized via the standard big-M encoding using $r_{t,k}, r_{t',k}$).

### 5.10 Delay Definition

$$
\text{delay}_{t,s} \;\ge\; \text{arr}_{t,s} - \text{sch\_arr}_{t,s} \qquad \forall\, t \in T,\; s \in S
$$

$$
\text{delay}_{t,s} \;\ge\; 0 \qquad \forall\, t \in T,\; s \in S
$$

### 5.11 Origin and Destination Anchors

$$
\text{arr}_{t,o_t} \;=\; \text{sch\_arr}_{t,o_t} \qquad \forall\, t \in T
$$

$$
\text{dep}_{t,\text{dst}_t} \;=\; \text{sch\_dep}_{t,\text{dst}_t} \qquad \forall\, t \in T
$$

### 5.12 Energy Consumption (PWL-linearized)

Convex combination of breakpoints:

$$
\sum_{p \in P} \lambda_{t,k,b,i,p} \;=\; 1 \qquad \forall\, t,k,b,i
$$

Reconstruction of $v$ and $v^2$:

$$
v_{t,k,b,i} \;=\; \sum_{p \in P} \lambda_{t,k,b,i,p}\, v_p \qquad \forall\, t,k,b,i
$$

$$
v^{\text{sq}}_{t,k,b,i} \;=\; \sum_{p \in P} \lambda_{t,k,b,i,p}\, v_p^{\text{sq}} \qquad \forall\, t,k,b,i
$$

Energy definition:

$$
e_{t,k,b,i} \;=\; \bigl(e_0 + e_1\, v_{t,k,b,i} + e_2\, v^{\text{sq}}_{t,k,b,i} + e_3\, a_{t,k,b,i}\bigr)\,\Delta t \qquad \forall\, t,k,b,i
$$

(For a tighter formulation, add the adjacent-convexity constraint $\lambda_{t,k,b,i,p} \le \lambda_{t,k,b,i,p-1} + \lambda_{t,k,b,i,p+1}$ to enforce SOS2 behavior.)

### 5.13 Headway (minimum time gap between consecutive trains)

For any two trains sharing the same direction, the later arrival must respect the headway:

$$
\text{arr}_{t',s} - \text{arr}_{t,s} \;\ge\; \tau - M\bigl(1 - y_{t,t',s}\bigr) \qquad \forall\, t,t' \in T,\; \text{dir}_t = \text{dir}_{t'},\; s \in S
$$

### 5.14 Ordering Variables (resolve pairwise conflicts)

$$
y_{t,t',k,b,i} + y_{t',t,k,b,i} \;=\; 1 \qquad \forall\, t < t',\; k \in K,\; b \in B_k,\; i \in I
$$

Linking ordering to headway at the block level (alternative to 5.13):

$$
\text{arr}_{t',s} - \text{arr}_{t,s} \;\ge\; \tau - M\bigl(1 - y_{t,t',k,b,i}\bigr) - M\bigl(1 - x_{t,k,b,i}\bigr) - M\bigl(1 - x_{t',k,b,i}\bigr)
$$
$$
\forall\, t < t',\; k,b,\; i,\; s
$$

### 5.15 Cancellation

If a train is cancelled, it occupies no block:

$$
x_{t,k,b,i} \;\le\; 1 - \text{cancel}_t \qquad \forall\, t \in T,\; k \in K,\; b \in B_k,\; i \in I
$$

Cancelled trains are exempt from arrival/departure anchors:

$$
\text{arr}_{t,o_t} \;\le\; \text{sch\_arr}_{t,o_t} + M\,\text{cancel}_t \qquad \forall\, t \in T
$$

$$
\text{arr}_{t,o_t} \;\ge\; \text{sch\_arr}_{t,o_t} - M\,\text{cancel}_t \qquad \forall\, t \in T
$$

(and analogously for $\text{dep}_{t,\text{dst}_t}$).

---

## 6. Explanation of Model Elements

**Decision variables.** $x_{t,k,b,i}$ encodes the spatio-temporal trajectory of every train at the granularity of one block and one time interval. $v_{t,k,b,i}$ and $a_{t,k,b,i}$ capture the speed profile, which is the key lever for energy-efficient rescheduling. $\text{arr}_{t,s}$ and $\text{dep}_{t,s}$ are the macroscopic timing variables at stations; $\text{delay}_{t,s}$ measures schedule deviation. $y_{t,t',k,b,i}$ resolves pairwise conflicts deterministically, $r_{t,k}$ enables bidirectional running on single-track sections, and $\text{cancel}_t$ is the last-resort option.

**Objective.** A weighted sum balances three competing goals: passenger-oriented punctuality ($\alpha \cdot \text{delay}$), operational cost via energy ($\beta \cdot e$), and service cancellation ($\gamma \cdot \text{cancel}$). The weights $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ are tunable by the dispatcher.

**Constraints.**
- **(5.1)–(5.2)** enforce track capacity: at most one train per direction per block-time, and no opposite-direction conflicts.
- **(5.3)** guarantees physically feasible motion — a train can advance at most one block per interval and cannot teleport.
- **(5.4)–(5.6)** couple speed and acceleration to the discrete-time motion model, with hard physical limits.
- **(5.7)** enforces minimum and maximum dwell times at stations.
- **(5.8)** models the partial blockage: during $[t_d^{\text{start}}, t_d^{\text{end}}]$, the disrupted segment is unusable in direction $\text{dir}_d$ unless the train reroutes.
- **(5.9)** activates bidirectional running: rerouting flips the effective direction, allowing the train to use the otherwise-disrupted (or congested) track.
- **(5.10)–(5.11)** define delay and anchor the schedule at the journey endpoints.
- **(5.12)** linearizes the quadratic energy function $e_0 + e_1 v + e_2 v^2 + e_3 a$ using a PWL approximation with breakpoints $v_p$, preserving linearity of the overall model.
- **(5.13)–(5.14)** enforce the safety headway $\tau$ between consecutive trains in the same direction, using ordering variables to linearize the conditional.
- **(5.15)** allows full cancellation as a feasible (but expensive) recourse when no feasible routing exists.

**Linearity.** All constraints are linear in the decision variables. The only originally nonlinear term, $v^2$, is replaced by the auxiliary $v^{\text{sq}}$ reconstructed via the convex combination $\lambda$ over precomputed breakpoints $v_p^{\text{sq}}$, which is a standard PWL technique that preserves MILP tractability.

delay_{t,s} ≥ dep_{t,s} - sch_dep_{t,s}

arr_{t',s} - arr_{t,s} ≥ τ or arr_{t,s} - arr_{t',s} ≥ τ (using y variables)

For opposite direction trains:
Spatial headway constraint

y_{t,t',k,b,i} + y_{t',t,k,b,i} = 1 (for trains using same block)
y_{t,t',k,b,i} + y_{t',t,k,b,i} ≥ x_{t,k,b,i} + x_{t',k,b,i} - 1

So the lower bound LU is less than the true value. Good.

So the McCormick envelope is:

But the tighter bounds are:

- The upper bound is the minimum of the two lines

Generate a complete MILP model for the Train Rescheduling and Speed Management Problem (TRSMP) under partial segment blockages in high-speed railways.

PROBLEM CONTEXT:
- High-speed railway line with bidirectional traffic on a double-track line
- A partial segment blockage disrupts one track of a specific segment for a time window
- Trains can be rerouted to the opposite (undisrupted) track during the disruption
- Need to integrate train rescheduling (TRP) with speed management (TSMP)

DECISIONS:
1. Retiming: adjust arrival/departure times at stations
2. Reordering: change the order of trains on shared track sections
3. Rerouting: divert trains to opposite track during disruption
4. Cancellation: optionally cancel some train services
5. Speed profiles: determine speed in each block/time interval

KEY ASSUMPTIONS (mark as assumptions):
- Single high-speed line with stations S = {1,...,|S|} ordered along the line
- Each segment k connects station k to station k+1
- Each segment is divided into |B_k| blocks of equal length for fine-grained scheduling
- Discrete time horizon I = {1,...,|I|} with time step Δt
- Trains have fixed origin-destination pairs and directions
- Trains cannot overtake within a block (only at stations)
- Constant acceleration/deceleration within each block-time cell
- Energy consumption follows a quadratic function of speed: e = (e0 + e1*v + e2*v^2 + e3*a)*Δt
- Minimum headway time τ between consecutive trains in same direction
- Minimum spatial headway for opposite direction trains
- Dwell times at stations are bounded: dwell_min ≤ dep - arr ≤ dwell_max

SETS:
- T: set of trains
- S: set of stations
- K: set of segments (K = {1,...,|S|-1})
- B_k: set of blocks in segment k
- I: set of time intervals
- D = {1, 2}: directions (1 = up, 2 = down)

PARAMETERS:
- L_k: length of segment k
- L_{k,b}: length of block b in segment k
- v_max, v_min: max/min speed
- a_max, b_max: max acceleration/deceleration
- τ: minimum headway time
- τ_space: minimum spatial headway for opposite direction
- t_d_start, t_d_end: disruption time window
- k_d: disrupted segment
- dir_d: direction of disrupted track
- dwell_min, dwell_max: min/max dwell times
- e0, e1, e2, e3: energy coefficients
- sch_arr_{t,s}, sch_dep_{t,s}: scheduled times
- o_t, dst_t, dir_t: origin, destination, direction of train t
- M: large constant (big-M)
- Δt: time step duration

VARIABLES:
- x_{t,k,b,i} ∈ {0,1}: 1 if train t occupies block b of segment k at time i
- v_{t,k,b,i} ≥ 0: speed of train t in block b of segment k at time i
- a_{t,k,b,i}: acceleration of train t (can be negative for deceleration)
- arr_{t,s} ≥ 0: actual arrival time at station s
- dep_{t,s} ≥ 0: actual departure time at station s
- delay_{t,s} ≥ 0: delay at station s
- e_{t,k,b,i} ≥ 0: energy consumption
- y_{t,t',k,b,i} ∈ {0,1}: 1 if train t precedes train t' in block b at time i
- r_{t,k} ∈ {0,1}: 1 if train t uses opposite track on segment k
- cancel_t ∈ {0,1}: 1 if train t is cancelled
- u_{t,k,b,i} ∈ {0,1}: 1 if train t enters block b of segment k at time i

OBJECTIVE:
Minimize weighted sum of:
- Total passenger delay: α * Σ_{t∈T, s∈S} delay_{t,s}
- Total energy consumption: β * Σ_{t,k,b,i} e_{t,k,b,i}
- Number of cancellations: γ * Σ_t cancel_t

CONSTRAINTS (must include):
1. Block occupation: at most one train per direction per block-time cell
2. Bidirectional conflict: opposite direction trains cannot share block at same time
3. Flow conservation: trains move sequentially through blocks
4. Train dynamics: speed transitions respect acceleration limits
5. Speed limits: v_min ≤ v_{t,k,b,i} ≤ v_max
6. Dwell time constraints at stations
7. Disruption constraints: no train on disrupted track during disruption window
8. Rerouting logic: if r_{t,k}=1, train uses opposite track
9. Delay definition
10. Origin/destination constraints
11. Energy consumption model (linearized)
12. Headway constraints (temporal and spatial)
13. Ordering constraints for reordering
14. Cancellation logic

The model should be a complete, linear MILP formulation with all equations clearly specified.

Generate a complete MILP model for the Train Rescheduling and Speed Management Problem (TRSMP) under partial segment blockages in high-speed railways.

PROBLEM CONTEXT:
- High-speed railway line with bidirectional traffic on a double-track line
- A partial segment blockage disrupts one track of a specific segment for a time window
- Trains can be rerouted to the opposite (undisrupted) track during the disruption
- Need to integrate train rescheduling (TRP) with speed management (TSMP)

DECISIONS:
1. Retiming: adjust arrival/departure times at stations
2. Reordering: change the order of trains on shared track sections
3. Rerouting: divert trains to opposite track during disruption
4. Cancellation: optionally cancel some train services
5. Speed profiles: determine speed in each block/time interval

KEY ASSUMPTIONS (mark as assumptions):
- Single high-speed line with stations S = {1,...,|S|} ordered along the line
- Each segment k connects station k to station k+1
- Each segment is divided into |B_k| blocks of equal length for fine-grained scheduling
- Discrete time horizon I = {1,...,|I|} with time step Δt
- Trains have fixed origin-destination pairs and directions
- Trains cannot overtake within a block (only at stations)
- Constant acceleration/deceleration within each block-time cell
- Energy consumption follows a quadratic function of speed: e = (e0 + e1*v + e2*v^2 + e3*a)*Δt
- Minimum headway time τ between consecutive trains in same direction
- Minimum spatial headway for opposite direction trains
- Dwell times at stations are bounded: dwell_min ≤ dep - arr ≤ dwell_max

SETS:
- T: set of trains
- S: set of stations
- K: set of segments (K = {1,...,|S|-1})
- B_k: set of blocks in segment k
- I: set of time intervals
- D = {1, 2}: directions (1 = up, 2 = down)

PARAMETERS:
- L_k: length of segment k
- L_{k,b}: length of block b in segment k
- v_max, v_min: max/min speed
- a_max, b_max: max acceleration/deceleration
- τ: minimum headway time
- τ_space: minimum spatial headway for opposite direction
- t_d_start, t_d_end: disruption time window
- k_d: disrupted segment
- dir_d: direction of disrupted track
- dwell_min, dwell_max: min/max dwell times
- e0, e1, e2, e3: energy coefficients
- sch_arr_{t,s}, sch_dep_{t,s}: scheduled times
- o_t, dst_t, dir_t: origin, destination, direction of train t
- M: large constant (big-M)
- Δt: time step duration

VARIABLES:
- x_{t,k,b,i} ∈ {0,1}: 1 if train t occupies block b of segment k at time i
- v_{t,k,b,i} ≥ 0: speed of train t in block b of segment k at time i
- a_{t,k,b,i}: acceleration of train t (can be negative for deceleration)
- arr_{t,s} ≥ 0: actual arrival time at station s
- dep_{t,s} ≥ 0: actual departure time at station s
- delay_{t,s} ≥ 0: delay at station s
- e_{t,k,b,i} ≥ 0: energy consumption
- y_{t,t',k,b,i} ∈ {0,1}: 1 if train t precedes train t' in block b at time i
- r_{t,k} ∈ {0,1}: 1 if train t uses opposite track on segment k
- cancel_t ∈ {0,1}: 1 if train t is cancelled
- u_{t,k,b,i} ∈ {0,1}: 1 if train t enters block b of segment k at time i

OBJECTIVE:
Minimize weighted sum of:
- Total passenger delay: α * Σ_{t∈T, s∈S} delay_{t,s}
- Total energy consumption: β * Σ_{t,k,b,i} e_{t,k,b,i}
- Number of cancellations: γ * Σ_t cancel_t

CONSTRAINTS (must include):
1. Block occupation: at most one train per direction per block-time cell
2. Bidirectional conflict: opposite direction trains cannot share block at same time
3. Flow conservation: trains move sequentially through blocks
4. Train dynamics: speed transitions respect acceleration limits
5. Speed limits: v_min ≤ v_{t,k,b,i} ≤ v_max
6. Dwell time constraints at stations
7. Disruption constraints: no train on disrupted track during disruption window
8. Rerouting logic: if r_{t,k}=1, train uses opposite track
9. Delay definition
10. Origin/destination constraints
11. Energy consumption model (linearized)
12. Headway constraints (temporal and spatial)
13. Ordering constraints for reordering
14. Cancellation logic

The model should be a complete, linear MILP formulation with all equations clearly specified.

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.

- Acceleration limits: -b_max ≤ a_{t,k,b,i} ≤ a_max
- Dwell time: dwell_min ≤ dep_{t,s} - arr_{t,s} ≤ dwell_max
- Disruption: x_{t,k_d,b,i} = 0 for i in disruption window if dir_t = dir_d
- Rerouting: if r_{t,k}=1, train uses opposite track
- Delay: delay_{t,s} ≥ arr_{t,s} - sch_arr_{t,s}
- Origin/destination: arr_{t,o_t} = sch_arr_{t,o_t}, dep_{t,dst_t} = sch_dep_{t,dst_t}
- Energy: e_{t,k,b,i} = (e0 + e1*v + e2*v^2 + e3*a)*Δt (linearized)
- Headway: arr_{t',s} - arr_{t,s} ≥ τ if same direction
- Ordering: y_{t,t',k,b,i} + y_{t',t,k,b,i} = 1 for conflicting trains
- Cancellation: if cancel_t=1, all x_{t,k,b,i}=0

Provide the COMPLETE model with all equations written out explicitly."}

Model 1:
# Train Rescheduling and Speed Management Problem (TRSMP) — Complete MILP Formulation

Below is the full mixed-integer linear program. All nonlinear terms (notably $v^2$ in the energy function) have been linearized via standard techniques (piecewise-linear approximation with binary selection variables and big-M).

---

## 1. Sets

| Symbol | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| $T$ | Set of trains, indexed by $t, t'$ |
| $S$ | Set of stations, indexed by $s$ |
| $K$ | Set of track segments, indexed by $k$ |
| $B_k$ | Set of blocks within segment $k$, indexed by $b$ |
| $I$ | Set of discrete time intervals, indexed by $i$ |
| $D=\{1,2\}$ | Set of travel directions (1 = nominal, 2 = opposite) |
| $N$ | Set of piecewise-linear segments for the $v^2$ approximation, indexed by $n$ |

---

## 2. Parameters

| Symbol | Description | Unit |
|--------|-------------|------|
| $L_k$ | Length of segment $k$ | km |
| $L_{k,b}$ | Length of block $b$ in segment $k$ | km |
| $v_{\max}, v_{\min}$ | Maximum / minimum allowable speed | km/h |
| $a_{\max}, b_{\max}$ | Maximum acceleration / deceleration | km/h per interval |
| $\tau$ | Minimum headway time | min |
| $t_d^{\text{start}}, t_d^{\text{end}}$ | Start / end of disruption window | interval index |
| $k_d$ | Disrupted segment | — |
| $\text{dir}_d \in D$ | Direction affected by disruption | — |
| $\text{dwell}_{\min}, \text{dwell}_{\max}$ | Min / max dwell time at stations | min |
| $e_0, e_1, e_2, e_3$ | Energy consumption coefficients | — |
| $\text{sch\_arr}_{t,s}, \text{sch\_dep}_{t,s}$ | Scheduled arrival / departure time | min |
| $o_t, \text{dst}_t$ | Origin / destination station of train $t$ | — |
| $\text{dir}_t \in D$ | Nominal direction of train $t$ | — |
| $M$ | Sufficiently large positive constant (big-M) | — |
| $\Delta t$ | Duration of one time interval | min |
| $v_n^L, v_n^U$ | Lower / upper speed bound of PWL segment $n$ | km/h |
| $\alpha_n, \beta_n$ | Slope / intercept of $v^2$ approximation on segment $n$ | — |
| $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ | Objective weights for delay, energy, cancellation | — |

---

## 3. Decision Variables

| Variable | Domain | Description |
|----------|--------|-------------|
| $x_{t,k,b,i}$ | $\{0,1\}$ | 1 if train $t$ occupies block $b$ of segment $k$ in interval $i$ |
| $v_{t,k,b,i}$ | $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ | Speed of train $t$ in block $(k,b)$ during interval $i$ |
| $a_{t,k,b,i}$ | $\mathbb{R}$ | Acceleration of train $t$ in block $(k,b)$ during interval $i$ |
| $\text{arr}_{t,s}$ | $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ | Actual arrival time of train $t$ at station $s$ |
| $\text{dep}_{t,s}$ | $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ | Actual departure time of train $t$ at station $s$ |
| $\text{delay}_{t,s}$ | $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ | Delay of train $t$ at station $s$ |
| $e_{t,k,b,i}$ | $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ | Energy consumed by train $t$ in block $(k,b)$ during interval $i$ |
| $w_{t,k,b,i}$ | $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ | Auxiliary variable $\approx v_{t,k,b,i}^2$ |
| $z_{t,k,b,i,n}$ | $\{0,1\}$ | 1 if PWL segment $n$ is active for the $v^2$ approximation |
| $y_{t,t',k,b,i}$ | $\{0,1\}$ | 1 if train $t$ precedes train $t'$ in block $(k,b)$ at interval $i$ |
| $r_{t,k}$ | $\{0,1\}$ | 1 if train $t$ is rerouted (uses opposite track) on segment $k$ |
| $\text{cancel}_t$ | $\{0,1\}$ | 1 if train $t$ is cancelled |

---

## 4. Objective Function

$$
\min \; Z \;=\; \alpha \sum_{t \in T}\sum_{s \in S} \text{delay}_{t,s} \;+\; \beta \sum_{t \in T}\sum_{k \in K}\sum_{b \in B_k}\sum_{i \in I} e_{t,k,b,i} \;+\; \gamma \sum_{t \in T} \text{cancel}_t
$$

---

## 5. Constraints

### 5.1 Block Occupation (one train per block-time-direction)

$$
\sum_{\substack{t \in T \\ \text{dir}_t = d}} x_{t,k,b,i} \;\le\; 1 \qquad \forall\, k \in K,\; b \in B_k,\; i \in I,\; d \in D
$$

### 5.2 Bidirectional Conflict (opposite-direction trains cannot share a block)

$$
x_{t,k,b,i} + x_{t',k,b,i} \;\le\; 1 \qquad \forall\, t,t' \in T:\; \text{dir}_t \neq \text{dir}_{t'},\; k \in K,\; b \in B_k,\; i \in I
$$

### 5.3 Flow Conservation (sequential block traversal within a segment)

$$
x_{t,k,b,i} \;\le\; x_{t,k,b-1,i} \qquad \forall\, t \in T,\; k \in K,\; b \in B_k \setminus \{1\},\; i \in I
$$

### 5.4 Train Dynamics (speed update)

$$
v_{t,k,b,i+1} \;=\; v_{t,k,b,i} + a_{t,k,b,i}\,\Delta t \qquad \forall\, t \in T,\; k \in K,\; b \in B_k,\; i \in I \setminus \{|I|\}
$$

### 5.5 Speed Limits

$$
v_{\min}\,x_{t,k,b,i} \;\le\; v_{t,k,b,i} \;\le\; v_{\max}\,x_{t,k,b,i} \qquad \forall\, t \in T,\; k \in K,\; b \in B_k,\; i \in I
$$

### 5.6 Acceleration Limits

$$
-b_{\max} \;\le\; a_{t,k,b,i} \;\le\; a_{\max} \qquad \forall\, t \in T,\; k \in K,\; b \in B_k,\; i \in I
$$

### 5.7 Dwell Time at Stations

$$
\text{dwell}_{\min} \;\le\; \text{dep}_{t,s} - \text{arr}_{t,s} \;\le\; \text{dwell}_{\max} \qquad \forall\, t \in T,\; s \in S
$$

### 5.8 Disruption (blocked segment/direction during disruption window)

$$
x_{t,k_d,b,i} \;=\; 0 \qquad \forall\, t \in T:\; \text{dir}_t = \text{dir}_d,\; b \in B_{k_d},\; i \in I:\; t_d^{\text{start}} \le i \le t_d^{\text{end}}
$$

### 5.9 Rerouting (if $r_{t,k}=1$, train uses opposite physical track)

Define the physical track used by train $t$ on segment $k$ as $p_{t,k} \in \{0,1\}$ (0 = track for direction 2, 1 = track for direction 1), where $p_{t,k} = \text{dir}_t \oplus r_{t,k}$ (XOR). Linearization:

$$
\begin{aligned}
p_{t,k} &\ge \text{dir}_t - r_{t,k} \\
p_{t,k} &\ge r_{t,k} - \text{dir}_t \\
p_{t,k} &\le \text{dir}_t + r_{t,k} \\
p_{t,k} &\le 2 - \text{dir}_t - r_{t,k}
\end{aligned}
\qquad \forall\, t \in T,\; k \in K
$$

Bidirectional conflict on the same physical track (replaces 5.2):

$$
x_{t,k,b,i} + x_{t',k,b,i} \;\le\; 1 + M\,|p_{t,k} - p_{t',k}| \qquad \forall\, t,t' \in T,\; k \in K,\; b \in B_k,\; i \in I
$$

with $|p_{t,k} - p_{t',k}|$ linearized via auxiliary variable $\delta_{t,t',k} \in \{0,1\}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\delta_{t,t',k} &\ge p_{t,k} - p_{t',k} \\
\delta_{t,t',k} &\ge p_{t',k} - p_{t,k} \\
|p_{t,k} - p_{t',k}| &= \delta_{t,t',k}
\end{aligned}
$$

### 5.10 Delay Definition

$$
\text{delay}_{t,s} \;\ge\; \text{arr}_{t,s} - \text{sch\_arr}_{t,s} \qquad \forall\, t \in T,\; s \in S
$$

### 5.11 Origin / Destination Pinning

$$
\text{arr}_{t,o_t} = \text{sch\_arr}_{t,o_t}, \qquad \text{dep}_{t,\text{dst}_t} = \text{sch\_dep}_{t,\text{dst}_t} \qquad \forall\, t \in T
$$

### 5.12 Energy Consumption (linearized)

$$
e_{t,k,b,i} \;=\; \bigl(e_0 + e_1\,v_{t,k,b,i} + e_2\,w_{t,k,b,i} + e_3\,a_{t,k,b,i}\bigr)\,\Delta t \qquad \forall\, t \in T,\; k \in K,\; b \in B_k,\; i \in I
$$

**Piecewise-linear approximation of $w = v^2$:**

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\sum_{n \in N} z_{t,k,b,i,n} = 1 &&\forall\, t,k,b,i \\
&v_n^L\,z_{t,k,b,i,n} \le v_{t,k,b,i} \le v_n^U\,z_{t,k,b,i,n} &&\forall\, t,k,b,i,\; n \in N \\
&w_{t,k,b,i} \ge \alpha_n\,v_{t,k,b,i} + \beta_n - M\,(1 - z_{t,k,b,i,n}) &&\forall\, t,k,b,i,\; n \in N \\
&w_{t,k,b,i} \le \alpha_n\,v_{t,k,b,i} + \beta_n + M\,(1 - z_{t,k,b,i,n}) &&\forall\, t,k,b,i,\; n \in N
\end{aligned}
$$

### 5.13 Headway at Stations (same direction)

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{arr}_{t',s} - \text{arr}_{t,s} &\ge \tau - M\,(1 - y_{t,t',s}) \\
\text{arr}_{t,s} - \text{arr}_{t',s} &\ge \tau - M\,y_{t,t',s} \\
y_{t,t',s} + y_{t',t,s} &= 1
\end{aligned}
\qquad \forall\, t,t' \in T:\; \text{dir}_t = \text{dir}_{t'},\; s \in S
$$

### 5.14 Block-Level Ordering (conflicting trains)

$$
y_{t,t',k,b,i} + y_{t',t,k,b,i} = 1 \qquad \forall\, t,t' \in T:\; t \neq t',\; k \in K,\; b \in B_k,\; i \in I
$$

with the linking constraint:

$$
x_{t,k,b,i} + x_{t',k,b,i} - 1 \;\le\; y_{t,t',k,b,i} + y_{t',t,k,b,i} \qquad \forall\, t,t' \in T,\; k \in K,\; b \in B_k,\; i \in I
$$

### 5.15 Cancellation

$$
x_{t,k,b,i} \;\le\; 1 - \text{cancel}_t \qquad \forall\, t \in T,\; k \in K,\; b \in B_k,\; i \in I
$$

### 5.16 Arrival/Departure Consistency

$$
\text{arr}_{t,s} \;\le\; \text{dep}_{t,s} \qquad \forall\, t \in T,\; s \in S
$$

$$
\text{arr}_{t,s+1} \;\ge\; \text{dep}_{t,s} \qquad \forall\, t \in T,\; s \in S \setminus \{|S|\}
$$

### 5.17 Block Traversal Time (speed–distance consistency)

$$
v_{t,k,b,i}\,\Delta t \;\le\; L_{k,b} + M\,(1 - x_{t,k,b,i}) \qquad \forall\, t \in T,\; k \in K,\; b \in B_k,\; i \in I
$$

### 5.18 Minimum Block Coverage (each block must be occupied long enough)

$$
\sum_{i \in I} x_{t,k,b,i} \;\ge\; \left\lceil \frac{L_{k,b}}{v_{\max}\,\Delta t} \right\rceil (1 - \text{cancel}_t) \qquad \forall\, t \in T,\; k \in K,\; b \in B_k
$$

### 5.19 Segment Entry/Exit (train must traverse every segment if not cancelled)

$$
\sum_{b \in B_k}\sum_{i \in I} x_{t,k,1,i} \;\ge\; 1 - \text{cancel}_t, \qquad \sum_{b \in B_k}\sum_{i \in I} x_{t,k,|B_k|,i} \;\ge\; 1 - \text{cancel}_t \qquad \forall\, t \in T,\; k \in K
$$

---

## 6. Explanation of Key Modeling Choices

| Element | Modeling rationale |
|---------|--------------------|
| **Time discretization** | The horizon is discretized into intervals of length $\Delta t$. This converts the continuous-time motion into a combinatorial problem suitable for MILP. |
| **Block occupation $x_{t,k,b,i}$** | Binary variable that captures both *where* and *when* a train is. All safety constraints (occupancy, headway, bidirectional conflict) are expressed through it. |
| **Speed/acceleration variables** | Indexed by $(t,k,b,i)$ so that the dynamics equation (5.4) is a pure linear recurrence. The big-M in (5.5) forces $v=0$ when the block is unoccupied. |
| **Energy linearization (5.12)** | The quadratic term $v^2$ is replaced by $w$ and approximated by a piecewise-linear function over $N$ segments. The binary $z_{t,k,b,i,n}$ selects the active segment; the four constraints enforce that $w$ equals the linear approximation on the active segment and is unconstrained otherwise. |
| **Rerouting (5.9)** | The XOR between $\text{dir}_t$ and $r_{t,k}$ is linearized with four inequalities defining $p_{t,k}$. The bidirectional conflict then uses $|p_{t,k}-p_{t',k}|$ (linearized via $\delta$) so that only trains on the *same physical track* compete for a block. |
| **Ordering variables $y$** | Used both at the station level (5.13) for headway and at the block level (5.14) to break symmetry between trains that would otherwise compete for the same resource. |
| **Cancellation (5.15)** | A single binary $\text{cancel}_t$ zeroes out all block occupations and contributes $\gamma$ to the objective, allowing the optimizer to trade off cancellation vs. delay/energy. |
| **Disruption (5.8)** | Directly forces $x=0$ for the affected segment, direction, and time window — the partial blockage is therefore "hard" (infeasible to traverse). |
| **Big-M usage** | All big-M terms are tightened by the natural bounds of the variables (e.g., $M \ge |I|\,\Delta t$ for time differences, $M \ge v_{\max}^2$ for the PWL approximation) to keep the LP relaxation strong. |

This model is a complete, linear MILP ready to be passed to any standard MILP solver (Gurobi, CPLEX, SCIP, HiGHS, etc.). The size of the instance is governed by $|T|\cdot|K|\cdot|B_k|\cdot|I|$ binary variables (block occupations) plus $|T|\cdot|K|\cdot|B_k|\cdot|I|\cdot|N|$ additional binaries for the PWL energy approximation.

Model 2:
# Train Rescheduling and Speed Management Problem (TRSMP) — Complete MILP Formulation

Below is the full mixed-integer linear program. All nonlinear terms (notably $v^2$) are linearized via a piecewise-linear (PWL) approximation with breakpoints, and all logical/implication conditions are encoded with big-M.

---

## 1. Sets

| Symbol | Description |
|---|---|
| $T$ | Set of trains, indexed by $t$ |
| $S$ | Set of stations, indexed by $s$ |
| $K$ | Set of segments, indexed by $k$ |
| $B_k$ | Set of blocks in segment $k$, indexed by $b$ |
| $I$ | Set of discrete time intervals, indexed by $i$ |
| $D=\{1,2\}$ | Directions (1 = nominal, 2 = opposite) |
| $P$ | Set of breakpoints for PWL of $v^2$, indexed by $p$ |

Auxiliary index sets:
- $I^{d} = \{i \in I : t_d^{\text{start}} \le i \le t_d^{\text{end}}\}$ — disruption window
- $T^{d} = \{t \in T : \text{dir}_t = \text{dir}_d\}$ — trains affected by disruption
- $\text{prev}(k,b), \text{next}(k,b)$ — predecessor/successor block of $(k,b)$ along the track

---

## 2. Parameters

| Symbol | Description |
|---|---|
| $L_k$ | Length of segment $k$ |
| $L_{k,b}$ | Length of block $b$ in segment $k$ |
| $v^{\max}, v^{\min}$ | Maximum / minimum speed |
| $a^{\max}, b^{\max}$ | Maximum acceleration / deceleration |
| $\tau$ | Minimum headway time |
| $t_d^{\text{start}}, t_d^{\text{end}}$ | Start/end of disruption window |
| $k_d$ | Disrupted segment |
| $\text{dir}_d$ | Disrupted direction |
| $\text{dwell}^{\min}, \text{dwell}^{\max}$ | Min/max dwell time at stations |
| $e_0, e_1, e_2, e_3$ | Energy consumption coefficients |
| $\text{sch\_arr}_{t,s}, \text{sch\_dep}_{t,s}$ | Scheduled arrival/departure times |
| $o_t, \text{dst}_t$ | Origin / destination station of train $t$ |
| $\text{dir}_t$ | Nominal direction of train $t$ |
| $M$ | Large positive constant (big-M) |
| $\Delta t$ | Duration of one time interval |
| $v_p, v_p^{\text{sq}}$ | Speed at breakpoint $p$ and its square ($v_p^{\text{sq}} = v_p^2$) |

---

## 3. Decision Variables

| Variable | Domain | Description |
|---|---|---|
| $x_{t,k,b,i}$ | $\{0,1\}$ | 1 if train $t$ occupies block $(k,b)$ at interval $i$ |
| $v_{t,k,b,i}$ | $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ | Speed of train $t$ in block $(k,b)$ at interval $i$ |
| $a_{t,k,b,i}$ | $\mathbb{R}$ | Acceleration of train $t$ in block $(k,b)$ at interval $i$ |
| $\text{arr}_{t,s}$ | $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ | Actual arrival time of train $t$ at station $s$ |
| $\text{dep}_{t,s}$ | $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ | Actual departure time of train $t$ at station $s$ |
| $\text{delay}_{t,s}$ | $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ | Delay of train $t$ at station $s$ |
| $e_{t,k,b,i}$ | $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ | Energy consumed by train $t$ in block $(k,b)$ at $i$ |
| $y_{t,t',k,b,i}$ | $\{0,1\}$ | 1 if $t$ is ordered before $t'$ in block $(k,b)$ at $i$ |
| $r_{t,k}$ | $\{0,1\}$ | 1 if train $t$ is rerouted in segment $k$ |
| $\text{cancel}_t$ | $\{0,1\}$ | 1 if train $t$ is cancelled |
| $\lambda_{t,k,b,i,p}$ | $[0,1]$ | PWL weight for breakpoint $p$ |
| $v^{\text{sq}}_{t,k,b,i}$ | $\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ | Auxiliary variable equal to $v_{t,k,b,i}^2$ |

---

## 4. Objective Function

$$
\min \; \alpha \sum_{t \in T}\sum_{s \in S} \text{delay}_{t,s} \;+\; \beta \sum_{t \in T}\sum_{k \in K}\sum_{b \in B_k}\sum_{i \in I} e_{t,k,b,i} \;+\; \gamma \sum_{t \in T} \text{cancel}_t
$$

where $\alpha, \beta, \gamma \ge 0$ are weighting coefficients.

---

## 5. Constraints

### 5.1 Block Occupation (single train per block-time per direction)

$$
\sum_{t \in T : \text{dir}_t = d} x_{t,k,b,i} \;\le\; 1 \qquad \forall\, k \in K,\; b \in B_k,\; i \in I,\; d \in D
$$

### 5.2 Bidirectional Conflict (opposite directions cannot share a block)

$$
x_{t,k,b,i} + x_{t',k,b,i} \;\le\; 1 \qquad \forall\, t,t' \in T,\; \text{dir}_t \ne \text{dir}_{t'},\; k \in K,\; b \in B_k,\; i \in I
$$

### 5.3 Flow Conservation (sequential movement through blocks)

A train may occupy block $(k,b)$ at time $i$ only if it was in $(k,b)$ or in a predecessor block at $i-1$:

$$
x_{t,k,b,i} \;\le\; x_{t,k,b,i-1} + x_{t,\text{prev}(k,b),i-1} \qquad \forall\, t \in T,\; k \in K,\; b \in B_k,\; i \in I \setminus \{0\}
$$

A train in $(k,b)$ at $i-1$ must be in $(k,b)$ or a successor block at $i$:

$$
x_{t,k,b,i-1} \;\le\; x_{t,k,b,i} + x_{t,\text{next}(k,b),i} \qquad \forall\, t \in T,\; k \in K,\; b \in B_k,\; i \in I \setminus \{0\}
$$

(For boundary blocks, $\text{prev}$ or $\text{next}$ is null and the corresponding term is dropped.)

### 5.4 Train Dynamics (speed update)

$$
v_{t,k,b,i+1} \;=\; v_{t,k,b,i} + a_{t,k,b,i}\,\Delta t \qquad \forall\, t \in T,\; k \in K,\; b \in B_k,\; i \in I \setminus \{\max I\}
$$

### 5.5 Speed Limits

$$
v^{\min}\, x_{t,k,b,i} \;\le\; v_{t,k,b,i} \;\le\; v^{\max}\, x_{t,k,b,i} \qquad \forall\, t,k,b,i
$$

### 5.6 Acceleration Limits

$$
-b^{\max}\, x_{t,k,b,i} \;\le\; a_{t,k,b,i} \;\le\; a^{\max}\, x_{t,k,b,i} \qquad \forall\, t,k,b,i
$$

### 5.7 Dwell Time at Stations

$$
\text{dwell}^{\min} \;\le\; \text{dep}_{t,s} - \text{arr}_{t,s} \;\le\; \text{dwell}^{\max} \qquad \forall\, t \in T,\; s \in S
$$

### 5.8 Disruption (blocked segment/direction/window)

Trains whose nominal direction equals the disrupted direction cannot occupy the disrupted segment during the disruption window unless they are rerouted:

$$
x_{t,k_d,b,i} \;\le\; r_{t,k_d} \qquad \forall\, t \in T^{d},\; b \in B_{k_d},\; i \in I^{d}
$$

### 5.9 Rerouting (use opposite track)

If $r_{t,k}=1$, train $t$ uses the opposite-direction track in segment $k$. The bidirectional conflict (5.2) is therefore conditioned on the *effective* direction:

$$
\text{eff\_dir}_{t,k} \;=\; \text{dir}_t\,(1 - r_{t,k}) + (3 - \text{dir}_t)\,r_{t,k}
$$

The conflict constraint becomes:

$$
x_{t,k,b,i} + x_{t',k,b,i} \;\le\; 1 + M\bigl(1 - [\text{eff\_dir}_{t,k} = \text{eff\_dir}_{t',k}]\bigr) \qquad \forall\, t,t',k,b,i
$$

where $[\cdot]$ is the indicator (linearized via the standard big-M encoding using $r_{t,k}, r_{t',k}$).

### 5.10 Delay Definition

$$
\text{delay}_{t,s} \;\ge\; \text{arr}_{t,s} - \text{sch\_arr}_{t,s} \qquad \forall\, t \in T,\; s \in S
$$

$$
\text{delay}_{t,s} \;\ge\; 0 \qquad \forall\, t \in T,\; s \in S
$$

### 5.11 Origin and Destination Anchors

$$
\text{arr}_{t,o_t} \;=\; \text{sch\_arr}_{t,o_t} \qquad \forall\, t \in T
$$

$$
\text{dep}_{t,\text{dst}_t} \;=\; \text{sch\_dep}_{t,\text{dst}_t} \qquad \forall\, t \in T
$$

### 5.12 Energy Consumption (PWL-linearized)

Convex combination of breakpoints:

$$
\sum_{p \in P} \lambda_{t,k,b,i,p} \;=\; 1 \qquad \forall\, t,k,b,i
$$

Reconstruction of $v$ and $v^2$:

$$
v_{t,k,b,i} \;=\; \sum_{p \in P} \lambda_{t,k,b,i,p}\, v_p \qquad \forall\, t,k,b,i
$$

$$
v^{\text{sq}}_{t,k,b,i} \;=\; \sum_{p \in P} \lambda_{t,k,b,i,p}\, v_p^{\text{sq}} \qquad \forall\, t,k,b,i
$$

Energy definition:

$$
e_{t,k,b,i} \;=\; \bigl(e_0 + e_1\, v_{t,k,b,i} + e_2\, v^{\text{sq}}_{t,k,b,i} + e_3\, a_{t,k,b,i}\bigr)\,\Delta t \qquad \forall\, t,k,b,i
$$

(For a tighter formulation, add the adjacent-convexity constraint $\lambda_{t,k,b,i,p} \le \lambda_{t,k,b,i,p-1} + \lambda_{t,k,b,i,p+1}$ to enforce SOS2 behavior.)

### 5.13 Headway (minimum time gap between consecutive trains)

For any two trains sharing the same direction, the later arrival must respect the headway:

$$
\text{arr}_{t',s} - \text{arr}_{t,s} \;\ge\; \tau - M\bigl(1 - y_{t,t',s}\bigr) \qquad \forall\, t,t' \in T,\; \text{dir}_t = \text{dir}_{t'},\; s \in S
$$

### 5.14 Ordering Variables (resolve pairwise conflicts)

$$
y_{t,t',k,b,i} + y_{t',t,k,b,i} \;=\; 1 \qquad \forall\, t < t',\; k \in K,\; b \in B_k,\; i \in I
$$

Linking ordering to headway at the block level (alternative to 5.13):

$$
\text{arr}_{t',s} - \text{arr}_{t,s} \;\ge\; \tau - M\bigl(1 - y_{t,t',k,b,i}\bigr) - M\bigl(1 - x_{t,k,b,i}\bigr) - M\bigl(1 - x_{t',k,b,i}\bigr)
$$
$$
\forall\, t < t',\; k,b,\; i,\; s
$$

### 5.15 Cancellation

If a train is cancelled, it occupies no block:

$$
x_{t,k,b,i} \;\le\; 1 - \text{cancel}_t \qquad \forall\, t \in T,\; k \in K,\; b \in B_k,\; i \in I
$$

Cancelled trains are exempt from arrival/departure anchors:

$$
\text{arr}_{t,o_t} \;\le\; \text{sch\_arr}_{t,o_t} + M\,\text{cancel}_t \qquad \forall\, t \in T
$$

$$
\text{arr}_{t,o_t} \;\ge\; \text{sch\_arr}_{t,o_t} - M\,\text{cancel}_t \qquad \forall\, t \in T
$$

(and analogously for $\text{dep}_{t,\text{dst}_t}$).

---

## 6. Explanation of Model Elements

**Decision variables.** $x_{t,k,b,i}$ encodes the spatio-temporal trajectory of every train at the granularity of one block and one time interval. $v_{t,k,b,i}$ and $a_{t,k,b,i}$ capture the speed profile, which is the key lever for energy-efficient rescheduling. $\text{arr}_{t,s}$ and $\text{dep}_{t,s}$ are the macroscopic timing variables at stations; $\text{delay}_{t,s}$ measures schedule deviation. $y_{t,t',k,b,i}$ resolves pairwise conflicts deterministically, $r_{t,k}$ enables bidirectional running on single-track sections, and $\text{cancel}_t$ is the last-resort option.

**Objective.** A weighted sum balances three competing goals: passenger-oriented punctuality ($\alpha \cdot \text{delay}$), operational cost via energy ($\beta \cdot e$), and service cancellation ($\gamma \cdot \text{cancel}$). The weights $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ are tunable by the dispatcher.

**Constraints.**
- **(5.1)–(5.2)** enforce track capacity: at most one train per direction per block-time, and no opposite-direction conflicts.
- **(5.3)** guarantees physically feasible motion — a train can advance at most one block per interval and cannot teleport.
- **(5.4)–(5.6)** couple speed and acceleration to the discrete-time motion model, with hard physical limits.
- **(5.7)** enforces minimum and maximum dwell times at stations.
- **(5.8)** models the partial blockage: during $[t_d^{\text{start}}, t_d^{\text{end}}]$, the disrupted segment is unusable in direction $\text{dir}_d$ unless the train reroutes.
- **(5.9)** activates bidirectional running: rerouting flips the effective direction, allowing the train to use the otherwise-disrupted (or congested) track.
- **(5.10)–(5.11)** define delay and anchor the schedule at the journey endpoints.
- **(5.12)** linearizes the quadratic energy function $e_0 + e_1 v + e_2 v^2 + e_3 a$ using a PWL approximation with breakpoints $v_p$, preserving linearity of the overall model.
- **(5.13)–(5.14)** enforce the safety headway $\tau$ between consecutive trains in the same direction, using ordering variables to linearize the conditional.
- **(5.15)** allows full cancellation as a feasible (but expensive) recourse when no feasible routing exists.

**Linearity.** All constraints are linear in the decision variables. The only originally nonlinear term, $v^2$, is replaced by the auxiliary $v^{\text{sq}}$ reconstructed via the convex combination $\lambda$ over precomputed breakpoints $v_p^{\text{sq}}$, which is a standard PWL technique that preserves MILP tractability.

# MILP Formulation for TRSMP

## 1. Sets and Indices
- T = {1, 2, ..., |T|}: set of trains, indexed by t
- S = {1, 2, ..., |S|}: set of stations, indexed by s
- K = {1, 2, ..., |K|}: set of segments, indexed by k
- B_k = {1, 2, ..., |B_k|}: set of blocks in segment k, indexed by b
- I = {1, 2, ..., |I|}: set of time intervals, indexed by i
- D = {1, 2}: set of directions, indexed by d
- P = {1, 2, ..., |P|}: set of breakpoints for piecewise linear approximation, indexed by p

## 2. Parameters
- L_k: length of segment k (km)
- L_{k,b}: length of block b in segment k (km)
- v_max, v_min: maximum and minimum speed (km/h)
- a_max: maximum acceleration (km/h²)
- b_max: maximum deceleration (km/h²)
- τ: minimum headway time (h or min)
- t_d_start, t_d_end: disruption start and end time
- k_d: disrupted segment
- dir_d: disrupted direction
- dwell_min, dwell_max: minimum and maximum dwell time at stations
- e0, e1, e2, e3: energy coefficients
- sch_arr_{t,s}, sch_dep_{t,s}: scheduled arrival and departure times
- o_t, dst_t: origin and destination stations of train t
- dir_t: direction of train t
- M: big-M constant
- Δt: time step duration
- v_p: speed at breakpoint p (for piecewise linear approximation)

## 3. Decision Variables
- x_{t,k,b,i} ∈ {0,1}: 1 if train t occupies block b of segment k at time interval i
- v_{t,k,b,i} ≥ 0: speed of train t in block b of segment k at time interval i
- a_{t,k,b,i}: acceleration of train t in block b of segment k at time interval i (free)
- arr_{t,s} ≥ 0: actual arrival time of train t at station s
- dep_{t,s} ≥ 0: actual departure time of train t at station s
- delay_{t,s} ≥ 0: delay of train t at station s
- e_{t,k,b,i} ≥ 0: energy consumption of train t in block b of segment k at time interval i
- y_{t,t',k,b,i} ∈ {0,1}: 1 if train t precedes train t' in block b of segment k at time interval i
- r_{t,k} ∈ {0,1}: 1 if train t uses segment k in its path
- cancel_t ∈ {0,1}: 1 if train t is cancelled
- λ_{t,k,b,i,p} ≥ 0: weight for breakpoint p (piecewise linear approximation)
- v²_{t,k,b,i} ≥ 0: auxiliary variable for v²
- w_{t,k,b,i}: auxiliary variable for v·a

## 4. Objective Function
minimize α · Σ_{t ∈ T, s ∈ S} delay_{t,s} + β · Σ_{t ∈ T, k ∈ K, b ∈ B_k, i ∈ I} e_{t,k,b,i} + γ · Σ_{t ∈ T} cancel_t

## 5. Constraints

### 5.1 Block Occupation (one train per block-time per direction)
Σ_{t ∈ T: dir_t = d} x_{t,k,b,i} ≤ 1, ∀ k ∈ K, b ∈ B_k, i ∈ I, d ∈ D

### 5.2 Bidirectional Conflict
x_{t,k,b,i} + x_{t',k,b,i} ≤ 1, ∀ t, t' ∈ T with dir_t ≠ dir_t', k ∈ K, b ∈ B_k, i ∈ I

### 5.3 Flow Conservation (within segment)
x_{t,k,b,i} - x_{t,k,b+1,i} = x_{t,k,b,i-1} - x_{t,k,b+1,i-1}, ∀ t ∈ T, k ∈ K, b ∈ B_k \ {|B_k|}, i ∈ I \ {1}

### 5.4 Train Dynamics (speed transitions)
v_{t,k,b,i} = v_{t,k,b,i-1} + a_{t,k,b,i} · Δt, ∀ t ∈ T, k ∈ K, b ∈ B_k, i ∈ I \ {1}

### 5.5 Speed Limits
v_min · x_{t,k,b,i} ≤ v_{t,k,b,i} ≤ v_max · x_{t,k,b,i}, ∀ t ∈ T, k ∈ K, b ∈ B_k, i ∈ I

dwell_min ≤ dep_{t,s} - arr_{t,s} ≤ dwell_max, ∀ t ∈ T, s ∈ S \ {o_t, dst_t}

Introduction

High-speed railways offer a rapid, efficient, and eco-friendly mode of transport that significantly enhances passenger mobility and drives regional economic growth. In recent years, the high-speed railway network has been undergoing continuing global expansion, resulting in increased traffic (Dal Sasso et al. 2022). In high-speed railway operations, train scheduling, as one of the most critical and challenging tasks, aims to execute and maintain a conflict-free timetable (Schälicke and Nachtigall 2025). However, the high-speed railway transport system is inherently complex and frequently subject to the impacts of unforeseen events, rendering the established timetable inexecutable. Based on severity, sudden events can be categorized into two types: disturbances and disruptions (Cacchiani et al. 2014). Disturbances are minor operational interruptions, such as slight delays during boarding, which can generally be managed within the existing timetable due to its inherent robustness. The core issue arising from minor disturbances is railway delay management (Flamini and Pacciarelli 2008; Schachtebeck and Schöbel 2010; Pellegrini, Marlière, and Rodriguez 2014). In contrast, disruptions are major operational interruptions causing substantial timetable modifications, that can severely affect train operations, leading to delays and increased operational costs (Kroon, Maróti, and Nielsen 2015; Borraz-Sánchez, Klabjan, and Uygur 2020; Croella et al. 2022). When a disruption occurs, some trains cannot travel normally in affected segments, leading to deviations from the scheduled times and rendering predesigned speed profiles inapplicable (Bärmann, Martin, and Schneider 2021). These events necessitate a systematic adjustment of operational strategies, including arrival and departure times adjustments (retiming), train order modifications (reordering), train reoute alterations (rerouting), or even train service cancellations, referred to as the train rescheduling problem (TRP) (D’Ariano et al. 2008; Veelenturf et al. 2016). Among disruptions, those caused by partial segment blockages occur commonly (Louwerse and Huisman 2014; Zhan et al. 2016). Such disruptions are often caused by factors such as equipment failures that prevent the normal passage of one side of the track. Trains are unable to pass through specific segments (i.e., disruption areas) at specific periods (i.e., during the disruption time window). Under such disruption scenarios, the TRP can incorporate local rerouting strategies. The rerouting strategy is designed to enhance operational flexibility and maintain unidirectional line capacity, allowing affected trains to divert to the opposite track within the disruption time window, thereby effectively mitigating delays. However, this strategy increases the complexity of the problem, as it introduces potential conflicts between bidirectional trains sharing the track resources, requiring the rescheduled timetable to precisely coordinate the paths and timing of bidirectional trains.

The implementation of a feasible rescheduling timetable of the TRP depends on the driving strategies at the train control level. Speed management translates operational-level dispatch instructions into precise and feasible train driving strategies, generating corresponding speed profiles to form the train speed management problem (TSMP) (Howlett, Pudney, and Albrecht 2022). The feasibility of a rescheduled timetable is directly contingent upon the feasibility of its corresponding speed profiles. This critical dependency highlights the necessity of incorporating speed management into disruption recovery frameworks. In partial segment blockage scenarios, trains must execute driving strategies based on optimized speed profiles of the TSMP, accelerating or decelerating in real time to meet the strict arrival/departure and inter-station running times requirements of the updated timetable, while passing through conflict zones. In this process, different speed profiles give rise to significant differences in energy consumption, thereby naturally establishing energy efficiency as an important co-optimization objective. Specifically, a disruption-affected train may either accelerate to arrive at the station earlier, which could necessitate an extended dwell time due to resource conflicts, or decelerate to align its arrival with the post-disruption recovery time, where these two strategies entail significantly distinct energy consumption patterns (Zhan et al. 2022).

The TRP and TSMP are closely related as inherent interdependencies exist between traffic-related properties (e.g., train running times, arrival and departure times) and train dynamics properties (e.g., train deceleration and acceleration) (Dong et al. 2021). Addressing these two problems separately fails to capture their intrinsic connection, may lead to rescheduling timetables that are infeasible at the control level, or to speed profiles that violate operational constraints, resulting in ineffective response to events (Yang et al. 2016). Consequently, the integrated optimization of train timetables and speed profiles under disruptions has emerged as a highly complex and challenging problem, referred to as the train rescheduling and speed management problem (TRSMP), attracting growing attention in high-speed railway operations research in recent years (e.g. Xu et al. 2017; Zhou et al. 2017; Xiu et al. 2025). In the context of partial blockages, the implementation of rerouting strategies further intensifies this complexity by amplifying potential conflicts between bidirectional trains, rendering the integrated problem a critical and yet unresolved challenge in the literature. Key challenges lie in synergistically resolving bidirectional train conflicts and the coupling between train rescheduling and speed management while rigorously ensuring the conflict-free operation of trains. This study proposes a novel integrated modeling and solution framework to address the TRSMP problem in a disruption caused by partial segment blockages, aiming to support coordinated rescheduling and control while facilitating rapid service recovery. Our scientific contribution is fivefold:

We introduce an innovative approach by integrating TRP and TSMP into a single framework, making this study one of the first to tackle both aspects simultaneously in the context of disruptions caused by partial segment blockages. This framework explicitly handles the dual challenges of bidirectional train conflict resolution on a shared track and the coupled decision-making between train rescheduling and speed control. It simultaneously optimizes the train times, orders, routes and speed profiles.

We propose a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that yields a conflict-free timetable and the corresponding executable speed profiles. Our formulation aligns train position and timing within the timetable with speed profiles, enhancing the accuracy and utility of the integrated model.

To tackle the computational complexity of the integrated model, we propose a decomposition-based solution method. We decompose the MILP into a reformulated integer programming (IP) model, focusing on train interactions, and a series of train plans, each addressing the operation of a single train. The integrated problem is transformed into a train plan selection problem. We have proved that the IP model with sufficiently fine interval plans is equivalent to the MILP.

We designed an adaptive iterative algorithm to address the combinatorial explosion of train plans and the potential infeasibility issues in the IP model. This algorithm iteratively refines the plan granularity within the neighborhood of the previous solution, thereby enhancing solution quality while maintaining computational efficiency. To further accelerate the process, we incorporate two tailored techniques with an adaptive refinement process and a local branching strategy.

Through extensive numerical experiments based on real-world scenarios, we validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. The results demonstrate that the adaptive algorithm accelerates the solution process for large-scale instances compared to solving the MILP or the IP models.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature on train rescheduling and integrated studies. Section 3 details the problem statement and assumptions. Section 4 outlines the MILP model formulation. Section 5 describes the solution framework. Section 6 presents case studies to demonstrate the practical application. Section 7 concludes the paper.
